_about: Hand-written key points for pyt-orthopaedics.html (27 Nov 2026, lead). Samples: FMGE recalls, no images; keys checked.
subject: Orthopaedics
intro: Orthopaedics in FMGE repeats the same pictures: the named fracture and its nerve, the classic sign, the bone tumour by age and site, and what to do first. These are the topics that keep coming back, most-asked first, with the one thing to remember about each.

ort.trauma.heal.note: Stages: haematoma, inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling. Healing is slowed by poor blood supply (scaphoid, femoral neck, lower tibia), movement at the fracture, infection, smoking and diabetes.
ort.trauma.heal.why: Fracture healing begins with a haematoma at the fracture site.

ort.trauma.comp.note: Delayed union, non-union (no healing after 6-9 months; hypertrophic or atrophic) and malunion. Avascular necrosis follows femoral neck, scaphoid and talus fractures. Sudeck (complex regional pain syndrome), myositis ossificans after elbow injuries, Volkmann ischaemic contracture after supracondylar fractures.

ort.trauma.cs.note: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch of the muscles, a tense swollen limb; pulses are lost late. Commonest after tibial fractures and tight casts. Split the cast and dressings, then urgent fasciotomy if pressure is over 30 mmHg (or within 30 of the diastolic).
ort.trauma.cs.why: Severe pain with pain on passive stretch and a tense limb after a tibial fracture is compartment syndrome.

ort.trauma.fat.note: Fat embolism syndrome 24-72 hours after long bone (femur) fractures: breathlessness and hypoxia, confusion, and a petechial rash on the chest, armpits and eyes (Gurd criteria). Prevent by early fixation; treat with oxygen and support.
ort.trauma.fat.why: Breathlessness, petechiae and confusion a day after a long bone fracture is fat embolism syndrome.

ort.trauma.poly.note: ATLS order: airway with cervical spine control, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure. Pelvic fractures can bleed massively: bind the pelvis. Damage control orthopaedics: external fixation first in unstable patients, definitive fixation later.

ort.nerve.rad.note: Radial nerve: injured with fractures of the humerus shaft (spiral groove) and by pressure in the arm (Saturday night palsy). Wrist drop, loss of finger and thumb extension, numb back of the first web space. Most recover; a cock-up splint meanwhile.
ort.nerve.rad.why: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus and is hurt in shaft fractures.

ort.nerve.uln.note: Ulnar nerve: injured at the elbow (medial epicondyle). Claw hand (ring and little fingers), wasting of the hand's small muscles, Froment sign (thumb flexes to grip paper because adductor pollicis is weak), numb little finger. Ulnar paradox: a lower lesion gives worse clawing.
ort.nerve.uln.why: Froment's sign shows weak adductor pollicis, which is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

ort.nerve.ax.note: Axillary nerve: injured in shoulder dislocation and fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. Loss of deltoid (abduction from 15° to 90°) and numbness over the 'regimental badge' area of the upper arm.
ort.nerve.ax.why: A surgical neck fracture injures the axillary nerve: lost abduction and numb outer upper arm.

ort.nerve.med.note: Median nerve: high lesions (supracondylar fracture) give the 'pointing index' (benediction hand on fist making) and lost thumb opposition; low lesions (carpal tunnel, wrist cuts) give an ape thumb and numb lateral three and a half fingers. Anterior interosseous branch: cannot make an 'OK' sign.
ort.nerve.med.why: An index finger that will not flex in a fist, weak opposition and lateral palm numbness mean a median nerve lesion.

ort.tum.gct.note: Giant cell tumour (osteoclastoma): young adults after the growth plate closes (20-40), at the epiphysis of the lower femur, upper tibia or lower radius. X-ray: lytic, eccentric, 'soap bubble'. Locally aggressive, can go to the lungs. Treated by curettage with bone graft or cement.

ort.tum.os.note: Osteosarcoma: teenagers, the metaphysis around the knee. Sunray spicules and Codman triangle (lifted periosteum) on X-ray; raised alkaline phosphatase. Spreads to the lungs. Linked to retinoblastoma (RB gene) and Paget disease in the elderly. Chemotherapy then limb-sparing surgery.
ort.tum.os.why: A distal femoral tumour with night pain in a teenager suggests osteosarcoma, which shows Codman's triangle.

ort.tum.ewing.note: Ewing sarcoma: children 5-15, the diaphysis of long bones and the pelvis. Fever and a raised ESR can mimic infection. Onion-peel periosteal reaction; small round blue cells, t(11;22). Very sensitive to radiotherapy.

ort.tum.oc.note: Osteochondroma (exostosis): the commonest benign bone tumour; a bony outgrowth with a cartilage cap pointing away from the joint, near the knee. Growth after skeletal maturity or a thick cap (over 2 cm) suggests change to chondrosarcoma.

ort.tum.ench.note: Enchondroma: a cartilage tumour inside the bones of the hand (the commonest hand bone tumour), with stippled calcification. Multiple: Ollier disease; with haemangiomas: Maffucci syndrome (higher risk of chondrosarcoma).

ort.tum.mm.note: Multiple myeloma: the commonest primary bone malignancy in adults over 50. Bone pain, anaemia, kidney failure, high calcium (CRAB); punched-out lytic skull lesions; bone scan may be cold, so a skeletal survey is used. M band on electrophoresis.
ort.tum.mm.why: Anaemia, bone pain, kidney problems and high calcium together point to multiple myeloma.

ort.paed.ctev.note: Club foot (CTEV): ankle equinus, hindfoot varus, forefoot adduction, midfoot cavus (CAVE). Ponseti method: serial casts from the first weeks (correct cavus first), percutaneous Achilles tenotomy, then a foot abduction brace for years.
ort.paed.ctev.why: Forefoot adduction, hindfoot varus, equinus and cavus together are congenital talipes equinovarus.

ort.paed.oi.note: Osteogenesis imperfecta: a defect in type I collagen; brittle bones with many fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, poor teeth. Can be mistaken for child abuse. Bisphosphonates reduce fractures.
ort.paed.oi.why: Recurrent fractures with blue sclerae come from a type I collagen gene mutation.

ort.om.ch.note: Chronic osteomyelitis: dead bone (sequestrum) inside new bone (involucrum), with sinuses discharging through cloacae. Staph aureus is the commonest cause (Salmonella in sickle cell). Treatment: surgical removal of the sequestrum plus long antibiotics. Long-standing sinuses can turn into squamous cell cancer (Marjolin ulcer).

ort.arth.oa.note: Osteoarthritis: wear of cartilage; pain worse with use, stiffness under 30 minutes. X-ray: narrowed joint space (medial in the knee, so bow legs, genu varum), osteophytes, sclerosis, cysts. Heberden nodes (DIP) and Bouchard nodes (PIP). Knee replacement for end-stage disease.
ort.arth.oa.why: The medial knee compartment wears first, so advanced knee osteoarthritis gives bow legs (genu varum).

ort.arth.ra.note: Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetrical small joints of the hands (MCP and PIP) and feet first, morning stiffness over an hour; spares the DIP joints. Anti-CCP is most specific. Deformities: swan neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation, Z thumb. Methotrexate is the first DMARD.
ort.arth.ra.why: Rheumatoid arthritis usually starts in the MCP and PIP joints of the hands.

ort.arth.as.note: Ankylosing spondylitis: young men, inflammatory back pain better with exercise, HLA-B27. Sacroiliitis first; bamboo spine and squaring of vertebrae later; reduced chest expansion; anterior uveitis. Schober test measures lumbar flexion. NSAIDs first, then anti-TNF drugs.

ort.arth.gout.note: Gout: monosodium urate crystals, needle-shaped and negatively birefringent. Big toe (podagra) first. Acute attack: NSAIDs, colchicine (blocks microtubules) or steroids; never start allopurinol during an attack. Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate, rhomboid and positively birefringent, the knee, chondrocalcinosis.
ort.arth.gout.why: Colchicine treats acute gout by blocking microtubule formation in neutrophils.

ort.met.op.note: DEXA T-score: −1 or above normal; −1 to −2.5 osteopenia; −2.5 or below osteoporosis. Fragility fractures: spine (wedge), hip, wrist (Colles). Calcium and vitamin D for all; bisphosphonates (alendronate) first-line drugs.
ort.met.op.why: A T-score of −2.5 or lower (here −2.7) is osteoporosis.

ort.met.rick.note: Rickets: vitamin D lack in children. Widened wrists, rachitic rosary, bow legs, Harrison sulcus, delayed fontanelle closure, frontal bossing. X-ray: cupping and fraying of the metaphysis. Blood: low calcium and phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase. In adults: osteomalacia.
ort.met.rick.why: Rickets is caused by vitamin D deficiency.

ort.met.hpt.note: Hyperparathyroidism in bone: subperiosteal bone loss on the radial side of the middle phalanges (the most specific X-ray sign), salt-and-pepper skull, brown tumours, osteitis fibrosa cystica. High calcium and PTH.

ort.fx.nof.note: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures cut the blood supply (medial circumflex femoral artery): avascular necrosis and non-union. Young patients: urgent closed or open reduction and internal fixation to save the head. Elderly displaced fractures: hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement. Leg is short and externally rotated.
ort.fx.nof.why: In a young adult the femoral head is saved by reduction and internal fixation as soon as possible.

ort.fx.it.note: Intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular, so the blood supply is kept and they heal well (but can malunite into varus). Elderly women after a fall; marked external rotation and shortening. Fixed with a dynamic hip screw or a proximal femoral nail.

ort.fx.sc.note: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus: the commonest elbow fracture in children, after a fall on the outstretched hand (extension type). Risks: brachial artery injury and Volkmann ischaemic contracture, median and anterior interosseous nerve injury, cubitus varus (gunstock deformity) from malunion.

ort.fx.colles.note: Colles fracture: lower radius within 2.5 cm of the wrist, the fragment tilted back (dinner-fork deformity); older women after a fall on the outstretched hand. Complications: malunion (the commonest), median nerve compression, rupture of extensor pollicis longus, Sudeck atrophy. Smith fracture tilts forward.
ort.fx.colles.why: The median nerve is the nerve most often affected after a Colles fracture.

ort.fx.scaph.note: Scaphoid: the commonest carpal fracture; fall on the outstretched hand, tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Early X-rays can be normal: treat as a fracture and repeat X-ray (or MRI). Blood enters from the far end, so the proximal pole can die (avascular necrosis) or not unite.
ort.fx.scaph.why: Pain at the base of the thumb after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests a scaphoid fracture.

ort.fx.gal.note: Galeazzi: fracture of the radius shaft with dislocation of the lower radio-ulnar joint (needs open fixation). Monteggia: fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head (watch the posterior interosseous nerve). Memory aid: 'GRUM' - Galeazzi radius, ulna Monteggia.

ort.joint.shd.note: Anterior dislocation is the commonest (flattened shoulder, axillary nerve risk); Bankart and Hill-Sachs lesions cause recurrence. Posterior dislocation after seizures or electric shock: arm held internally rotated, 'light bulb' sign on X-ray. Reduction: Kocher or traction methods.
ort.joint.shd.why: Shoulder pain after a seizure is the classic story of posterior dislocation.

ort.joint.rc.note: Supraspinatus is the most often torn rotator cuff tendon. Painful arc between 60° and 120° of abduction; drop arm test for a full tear. MRI or ultrasound to confirm. Older patients often manage with physiotherapy; repair for active patients.
ort.joint.rc.why: Supraspinatus is the rotator cuff tendon most commonly torn.

ort.joint.knee.note: ACL tear: a twisting injury with a pop and swelling within hours (haemarthrosis); Lachman test is the most sensitive. PCL: dashboard injury, posterior sag. Medial collateral: valgus stress. Unhappy triad (O'Donoghue): ACL, MCL and medial meniscus. MRI is the investigation of choice.
ort.joint.knee.why: A twist with a pop and quick swelling is an anterior cruciate ligament tear.

ort.joint.men.note: Meniscal tears: twisting on a bent knee; locking, clicking, joint line tenderness, swelling the next day. McMurray and Apley tests. The medial meniscus tears more often (it is fixed to the medial ligament). Bucket-handle tears lock the knee. MRI; arthroscopic repair or trimming.
ort.joint.men.why: The McMurray test checks for a meniscal tear.

ort.spine.disc.note: Commonest at L4-L5 and L5-S1, usually posterolateral, pressing on the lower root (L5 or S1). Straight leg raising test positive. Cauda equina syndrome (saddle numbness, bladder and bowel trouble) needs emergency surgery. MRI is the investigation of choice.

ort.spine.spl.note: Spondylolisthesis: forward slip of one vertebra on the one below, most often L5 on S1. Spondylolysis: a defect in the pars interarticularis, 'Scottie dog with a collar' on an oblique X-ray. Graded by Meyerding by the percentage of slip.
ort.spine.spl.why: Forward displacement of L5 over S1 is spondylolisthesis.

ort.spine.tb.note: Pott spine: the commonest site of skeletal TB, usually the thoracolumbar spine. Starts at the disc and the vertebral endplates (paradiscal), the disc space narrows, a cold abscess forms (psoas abscess), vertebrae collapse into a kyphosis (gibbus). Paraplegia can follow. MRI is the investigation of choice; anti-TB drugs, surgery for paraplegia.
ort.spine.tb.why: A gibbus (sharp angular kyphosis) is the classic deformity of spinal tuberculosis.
